text:
# Short answer

For a typical full-size fridge, get a pure sine wave power station with **at least 1,300 W surge** and about **1,000 Wh** for most of a day. For a full 24 hours with some margin, get about **1,500-2,000 Wh**. Plan on roughly 2,800 Wh for two days.

## The three checks

1. **Continuous watts:** A full-size fridge runs at about 100-250 W, so almost any 1,000 W-class station clears this ([BlackBox Supplies](https://www.blackboxsupplies.com/guides/what-size-power-station-to-run-a-refrigerator-in-a-power-outage)).
2. **Surge watts:** The compressor spikes on startup. Sources put it at roughly 1,000-1,300 W for typical fridges and up to 2,400 W for large or older ones ([HomeGridHQ](https://www.homegridhq.com/watts/fridge/), [BlackBox Supplies](https://www.blackboxsupplies.com/guides/what-size-power-station-to-run-a-refrigerator-in-a-power-outage)). Surge is the spec that most often makes a station fail, even with plenty of battery. Large French-door or older fridges need the higher end.
3. **Watt-hours:** The compressor cycles on only about a third of the time. One estimate for a typical ENERGY STAR fridge is about 41 W average, or around 1,400 Wh per day after inverter losses and 20% headroom ([powerstations.reviews](https://powerstations.reviews/guides/power-station-for-a-refrigerator)). Other sources use 50-70 W average, so I'd size toward the higher figure if your fridge is older or has an ice maker.

## Rough runtimes

| Station capacity | Approx. runtime for a typical fridge |
|---|---|
| ~770 Wh | ~12 hours |
| ~1,000 Wh | ~17 hours |
| ~1,500 Wh | ~25 hours |
| ~2,000 Wh | ~33 hours |

These come from HomeGridHQ's estimate, which assumes 85% inverter efficiency and a 35% duty cycle. Hot kitchens, frequent door openings and defrost cycles shorten them. Keeping the door closed helps a lot.

## Getting your own number

- Find your fridge's yellow EnergyGuide label: kWh per year × 1,000 ÷ 8,760 gives average watts.
- Multiply by the hours you need, divide by 0.85 for inverter losses, then add 20% headroom.
- Check the fridge's manual for startup watts. Compare it with the station's surge rating, not only its continuous rating.
- Look for **pure sine wave** output, which is preferred for compressor motors.

## Options

- **~1,000 Wh class (most of a day):** BLUETTI AC180 (1,152 Wh, 1,800 W, 2,700 W peak), Jackery Explorer 1000 v2, and EcoFlow RIVER 2 Pro are the picks in [BlackBox Supplies' guide](https://www.blackboxsupplies.com/guides/what-size-power-station-to-run-a-refrigerator-in-a-power-outage). Their price ranges there are about $370-800. That page doesn't give direct product links, so check current prices on each maker's site or Amazon. The AC180 is a bit above 1,000 Wh, but a 1,000 Wh unit gets you about 17 hours, so it falls short of a full day.
- **~2,000 Wh class (a full day plus margin):** [BLUETTI AC200L](https://dealectric.com/go/bluetti-ac200l) has 2,048 Wh, 2,400 W continuous, and can be expanded up to 8 kWh. It's listed at $899, with a 5% code (AFF5OFF) taking $44.95 off. That link is an affiliate link. The [Anker SOLIX S2000](https://www.ankersolix.com/blogs/portable-power-station/portable-power-station-for-refrigerator) (2,010 Wh, 1,500 W, 3,000 W peak) is another option. Anker's page lists it at $699.99 after coupon, but I didn't have a direct product link.

If you also want to run other things, like a router, lights or a medical device, add their watts and watt-hours to the totals above. For outages longer than two days, you'd want solar input or an expandable unit.
